## Our data and goal
We'll use every Chicago Airbnb listing scraped by [Inside Airbnb](https://insideairbnb.com/get-the-data/) in September 2026 to build and tune a non-parametric model of nightly `price` using a regression tree (or decision tree, same thing). I've trimmed it to 18 columns and dropped the 1% of listings priced over $1,500.

```{r, eval=F}
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(skimr)

airbnb = read.csv('https://ec242.netlify.app/data/airbnb_chicago.csv')
```

```{r, echo=F, include=F}
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(skimr)

airbnb = read.csv(here('data/airbnb_chicago.csv'))
```

```{r, echo=F, fig.width=5, fig.height=6, fig.align='center', dev.args=list(bg='grey10')}
ggplot(airbnb %>% arrange(price), aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = price)) +
  geom_point(size = .5, alpha = .8) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", option = "plasma", name = "Price per night",
                        labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "grey10", color = NA),
        legend.text = element_text(color = "grey85"),
        legend.title = element_text(color = "grey85"),
        plot.title = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 16),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey70"),
        plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)) +
  labs(title = "7,116 Chicago Airbnb listings", subtitle = "September 2026")
```

## Guess the price

Here are three real listings. Write down a nightly price for each one.

```{r}
guess = airbnb[c(351, 7006, 1082), ]
```

```{r, echo=F}
knitr::kable(guess %>%
               dplyr::mutate(listing = c("A", "B", "C")) %>%
               dplyr::select(listing, room_type, accommodates, bedrooms, bathrooms, minimum_nights,
                             number_of_reviews, superhost, host_listings),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

We've learned that our RMSE calculations have a hard time with `NA`s in the data. So let's use the `skim` output to tell us which variables have too many `NA` (see `n_missing`) values and should be dropped. Let's set a high bar here, and drop anything that isn't 100% complete. Of course, there are other things we can do (impute the `NA`s, or make dummies for them), but for now, it's easiest to drop them.

Remember, `skim()` is for your own exploration, it's not something that you should include in your output.

```{r, eval=F}
skim(airbnb)
```

The only two variables that aren't 100% complete are `review_scores_rating` and `reviews_per_month`, so those are the ones we drop. We also drop `listing_url`. It is a web address, not a predictor.

```{r, echo=T, include=T}
airbnb_clean = airbnb %>%
  dplyr::select(-review_scores_rating, -reviews_per_month, -listing_url)
```

Once cleaned, we should be able to use `rpart(price ~ ., data = airbnb_clean)` and not have any `NA`s in our prediction. That's what we'll do in our first Breakout.

::: {.callout-note}

## TRY IT

### Predicting price

I'm going to have you form groups of 2-3 to work on live-coding. One person in the group will need to have Rstudio up, be able to share screen, and have the correct packages loaded (`rpart` and `rpart.plot`, plus `dplyr` and `skimr`). Copy the `rmse` and `get_rmse` code into a blank R script (you don't have to use RMarkdown, just use a blank R script and run from there). You'll also want to have these functions from last week loaded:

```{r}
rmse = function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted) ^ 2))
}
```

```{r}
get_rmse = function(model, data, response) {
  rmse(actual = subset(data, select = response, drop = TRUE),
       predicted = predict(model, data))
}
```


For the first breakout, all I want you to do is the following. We are trying to predict `price` for this exercise:

- Estimate a default regression tree on `airbnb_clean` using the default parameters (use the whole dataset for now, we'll train-test on the problem set). Call it `onetree`.
- Use `rpart.plot` to visualize your regression tree, and *talk through the interpretation* with each other.
- Calculate the RMSE for your regression tree.

We'll spend about 5 minutes on this. You may find something odd at first and may need to drop more variables...

```{r, echo=F, include=F, eval=T}
airbnb_clean$quote_per_night = NULL
airbnb_clean$estimated_revenue = NULL

onetree = rpart(price ~ ., data = airbnb_clean)
rpart.plot(onetree)
get_rmse(onetree, airbnb_clean, 'price')
```
**5 minutes**

### Breakout #1 discussion
Let's choose a group to share their plot and discuss the results. The odd thing you should have hit: `quote_per_night` is the nightly price from a booking quote, so the tree splits on it and nothing else. Drop it. Then look at `estimated_revenue`: what is it computed from? Drop that too (`airbnb_clean$estimated_revenue = NULL`), re-run, and we'll keep using `airbnb_clean` for the rest of today.

```{r, echo=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
rpart.plot(onetree, box.palette = "BuGn", type = 2, extra = 100, under = TRUE, roundint = FALSE, tweak = 1.1,
           split.fun = function(x, labs, digits, varlen, faclen) gsub(" room", "", labs))
```

- Who are the hosts with 89 or more listings, and why are they so expensive?
- Why would a private room with a one-night minimum cost more than one with a longer minimum?

### Check your guesses

```{r, eval=F}
my_guess = c(150, 300, 400)   # replace with your guesses for A, B, C

data.frame(listing = c("A", "B", "C"),
           you     = my_guess,
           tree    = predict(onetree, guess),
           actual  = guess$price)

rmse(guess$price, my_guess)
rmse(guess$price, predict(onetree, guess))
```

What was the RMSE of your guesses? What was the RMSE of the tree?

:::

## TRY IT

### Breakout #2: Find the deals

A deal is a listing with a price far below the tree's prediction.

- Add the tree's prediction to `airbnb` as a new column, `pred`.
- Make a new column, `deal = price - pred`.
- Keep the listings with at least 10 reviews. Sort them by `deal`.
- Open the `listing_url` for the top five. Why are they cheap?
- Why do the top deals all have the same prediction?

```{r, echo=F, include=F}
airbnb %>%
  mutate(pred = predict(onetree, airbnb),
         deal = price - pred) %>%
  filter(number_of_reviews >= 10) %>%
  arrange(deal) %>%
  select(price, pred, deal, accommodates, bathrooms, listing_url) %>%
  head(5)
```

**5 minutes**

:::

::: {.callout-note}

## TRY IT

### Breakout #3: Map the tree

Fit a tree on location only. Then predict a price for every point on a grid and plot it.

```{r, eval=F}
maptree = rpart(price ~ latitude + longitude, data = airbnb, cp = 0.005)

grid = expand.grid(longitude = seq(min(airbnb$longitude), max(airbnb$longitude), length.out = 300),
                   latitude  = seq(min(airbnb$latitude),  max(airbnb$latitude),  length.out = 300))
grid$pred = predict(maptree, grid)

ggplot(grid, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, fill = pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_point(data = airbnb, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, size = .1, alpha = .2) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_dollar())
```

- Why are all the edges straight lines?
- What does the tree predict for a listing in Lake Michigan? Why?
- Change `cp` to 0.002. What changes?

**5 minutes**

:::



### Side note: using `lapply` to repeat something
As we did in the last two labs, we'll use `lapply` to iterate over a wide range of "tuning parameters" to optimize our model (find the lowest test RMSE).

Once we have a list of things we want to iterate on, `lapply` lets us do something to each element of the list, and then returns a list of results (of the same length as the input). The arguments of `lapply` are (1) the list we want to iterate over, (2) the function we want to use, and, when needed, (3) other arguments to pass to the function (that are the same for every element in the list). The list we want to iterate over might be a list of models (as we do when we want to use `get_rmse` on each model), or it might be a list (or a vector that can be coerced to a list) of tuning parameters.

Let's say we wanted to repeat our **TRY IT** with the `cp` values of `c(0, .01, .02, .03)`. We could make a list of those values, and use `lapply` to run `rpart()` and use each of the 4 values of `cp`. One way we could try doing this would be something like:

```{r, eval = F}
myList = lapply(c(0, .01, .02, .03), rpart, formula = price ~ ., data = airbnb_clean, cp = ???)
```

The only problem here is that the first argument of `rpart` is not the `cp` parameter, so we can't just pass it in additional arguments.

Instead, we previously introduced the *anonymous function* in `lapply` as follows:

```{r, eval = F}
myList = lapply(c(0, .01, .02, .03), function(x){
  rpart(price ~ ., data = airbnb_clean, cp = x)
})
```

Well, it gets us the right answer, but whaaaaaat is going on? Curly brackets? `x`?

This is an "anonymous function", or a function created on the fly. Here's how it works in `lapply`:

- The first argument is the list you want to do something to (same as before)
- The second argument would usually be the function you want to apply, like `get_rmse`
- Here, we're going to ask R to *temporarily* create a function that takes one argument, `x`.
- `x` is going to be each element of the vector you're iterating over — here, each value of `cp`. (`myList` is what comes *out* of `lapply`, not what goes in.)
- Think of it as a loop: 
  - Take the first element of `c(0, .01, .02, .03)` and refer to it as `x`. Run the function's code.
  - Then it'll take the second element and refer to it as `x` and run the function's code.
  - Repeat until every element has been used.
- Once the anonymous function has been applied to `x`, the result is passed back and saved as the new element of the list output, always in the same position from where the `x` was taken.

The curly brackets are the temporary function you want to create.


So you can think of it like this:

````
x = 0
myList[[1]] = rpart(price ~ ., data = airbnb_clean, cp = x)

x = 0.01
myList[[2]] = rpart(price ~ ., data = airbnb_clean, cp = x)

x = 0.02
myList[[3]] = rpart(price ~ ., data = airbnb_clean, cp = x)
````

As long as every entry in the vector you iterate over is a valid value of `cp`, then you'll get the results in a list — here, a list of four fitted trees, not a list of `cp` values.  When the list holds single numbers instead of models, `unlist` coerces it to a vector. This is also the same way we get the RMSE, but instead of the anonymous function, we write one out and use that.

If you had a list of `rpart` objects and wanted to, say, extract the `cp` tuning parameter from each, you could also use an anonymous function. Each `rpart` object has a list called `control` that includes all of the control (tuning) parameters used in its estimation:

```{r, eval = F}
cpList = lapply(myList, function(y){
  y$control$cp
})

unlist(cpList)
```

Here is `lapply` at work. Each panel is the location tree from Breakout #3 at a different value of `cp`.

```{r, echo=F, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
cps = c(0.05, 0.01, 0.005, 0.001)
maptrees = lapply(cps, function(x){
  rpart(price ~ latitude + longitude, data = airbnb, cp = x)
})

grid = expand.grid(longitude = seq(min(airbnb$longitude), max(airbnb$longitude), length.out = 250),
                   latitude  = seq(min(airbnb$latitude),  max(airbnb$latitude),  length.out = 250))

leaves = sapply(maptrees, function(t){ sum(t$frame$var == "<leaf>") })
panel_labels = paste0("cp = ", cps, "\n", leaves, ifelse(leaves == 1, " rectangle", " rectangles"))

maps = lapply(seq_along(maptrees), function(i){
  grid %>% mutate(pred = predict(maptrees[[i]], grid), panel = panel_labels[i])
})

ggplot(bind_rows(maps), aes(x = longitude, y = latitude)) +
  geom_raster(aes(fill = pred)) +
  geom_point(data = airbnb, size = .05, alpha = .15, color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~factor(panel, levels = panel_labels), nrow = 1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_dollar(), name = "Predicted\nprice") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 4)))
```


::: {.callout-note}

## TRY IT

### Breakout #4
Using the loop method or the `lapply` method, generate 10 regression trees to explain `price` in `airbnb_clean`. You can iterate through values of `cp`, the complexity parameter, **or** `minsplit`, the minimum # of points a node has to have before `rpart` will even try to split it. If you vary `minsplit`, also set `cp = 0`, or the default `cp` will stop every tree at the same size.

**10 minutes**

### Breakout #4 discussion
We'll ask someone to share (a few of) their group's 10 regression trees using `rpart.plot`. Use our website zoom link to share.

## TRY IT

### Breakout #5 (if time)
Use `lapply` to get a list of your RMSE's (one for each of your models). The anonymous function may come in handy here (though it's not necessary). Note that we are not yet splitting into `test` and `train` (which you **will** need to do on your lab assignment). That matters for what the plot looks like: because these are RMSEs on the same data we fit, they'll keep falling as the trees get bigger (as `cp` goes to zero, or as `minsplit` shrinks), so there's no bottom of the U to find here. The U only shows up once the RMSE is calculated on data the tree hasn't seen. 

Once you have your list, **create the plot of RMSEs** similar to the one we made in last week's lab. Note: you can use `unlist(myRMSE)` to get a numeric vector of the RMSE's (as long as all of the elements in `myRMSE` are numeric). Then, it's a matter of plotting either with base `plot` or with `ggplot` (if you use `ggplot` you'll have to put the RMSEs in a data frame first, with a second column holding the `cp` or `minsplit` value that goes on the x-axis).


:::
